name: Vera Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy and I love it. I'm on software engineering, so it's lectures, labs and then a lot of building things in my flat with my two flatmates, who are on the same course. On Wednesdays I run a coding club for ten-year-olds at a community centre, which pays a bit and is hilarious. I use AI tools every day, for explaining things, testing ideas and debugging.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you build in your free time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's a rota app for the students' union food bank. Volunteers kept double-booking, so I made a simple page where they pick shifts. It took a weekend with an AI assistant doing the boring parts, and I checked everything it wrote. The food bank manager, Joy, cried a little, which was a lot for a rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, fair enough, but it's still useful. Even a small time saving adds up when you're building things. I'd tell my coding club kids it's a good helper but you still have to know what you're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the idea of big change. But money-wise I'd be fine. My dad's a ferry mechanic and my mum works as a teaching assistant, they pay part of my costs, and my tutoring covers my phone and food. A normal degree and a normal job market feel manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Keep the club, keep improving the food bank rota, and apply for summer internships in the spring. I'd use the AI tools a bit less for basics so I don't get lazy, because I noticed I reach for them too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored, which is a funny thing to admit. I do get anxious about money in general, but nothing special about this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you reach for AI too fast. What did you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really do check what it writes. My flatmate Kofi pasted a whole function in last week and it passed the test but crashed with real data. I'd rather use it like a quick junior who needs supervision than like a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure do your parents' jobs feel to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If tuition went up or my parents' hours got cut, I'd feel it quickly. But it's not on the horizon. Dad's ferry company just ordered a new boat, so he's busy, and Mum's school isn't losing staff. That makes me calmer than most of my friends.

say: I'd say it's **fair enough**: still useful, but not a revolution.
I'd tell my coding club kids to **know what they're doing** first.
think: I'd be **a bit disappointed**, because I like the idea of big change.
Money feels **manageable**, with my parents' help and tutoring income.
do: Keep the **coding club** and improve the food bank rota.
Apply for **summer internships** in the spring.
Use AI less for **basics** so I don't get lazy.
feel: **Calm**, maybe a little bored, with ordinary money worries.
S0.quote: I'd rather use it like a quick junior who needs supervision than like a teacher.
fieldNote: Vera is an **enthusiast with discipline**: she checks AI work and notices when she leans on it too much.
Her calm rests on **concrete security**, a busy ferry yard for her dad and a stable school for her mum.
She admits to being slightly disappointed that nothing changes, a mark of her adaptive side.

steps.text: Keep running the Wednesday coding club
Apply for summer internships in March
Write basic code by hand twice a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting, but only if people are looked after. If AI is doing writing, checking and coding in lots of jobs, then we should talk about a shorter working week and workers having a say in the tools. Otherwise it's just fewer people doing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'm not scared, but I'm aware. Junior software roles are the ones most at risk, and I'm training for exactly that. I think the people who can combine building, checking and talking to humans will be fine, and I'm putting myself in that group, which might be optimism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further into it, building real projects with AI, and I'd get one that people actually use, like the food bank app. I'd choose modules about how systems fail, since someone has to check them. And I'd keep the coding club, because teaching is a skill the tools don't replace easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually, and kind of excited. I'm already in the world where I use it every day, so it's more of the same, just faster. I'd worry for people who don't get the chance to learn to use AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned people who don't get the chance to learn it. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm thinking of my gran, who lives with us and does the shopping online. She'd be the one who'd get stuck if customer services all turn into bots. I'd end up as her tech support, honestly, which I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If entry-level jobs shrink, what would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the entry-level jobs shrink, I'd probably do a placement year with a small company instead of a big one. Small firms let you touch everything, and they can't afford to hire a lot of juniors, so you'd stand out by being useful. That's my bet, anyway.

say: I'd say it's exciting if **people are looked after**, with a shorter working week.
I'd argue workers should have **a say** in the tools.
think: Junior software roles are **most at risk**, but combining building, checking and talking should help.
I know my confidence might just be **optimism**.
do: Build **real projects** that people use, like the food bank app.
Pick modules on **how systems fail**, since someone must check them.
Keep the **coding club**, because teaching is hard to replace.
feel: **Calm** and a little excited, since I already use it daily.
S1.quote: I'd worry for people who don't get the chance to learn to use AI tools.
fieldNote: Vera's calm is **earned by use**: she already works with the tools daily.
She worries for others, such as her gran, rather than herself, showing a progressive concern.
She has a specific strategy: a placement year with a **small firm** where juniors do everything.

steps.text: Build and launch one more app that real people use
Take the systems failure and testing module
Keep paid tutoring at the community centre club
Apply for a placement year at a small firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing in my lifetime and we have no plan. I'd go on and on, honestly. I'd say we need serious public ownership of the main systems and income support immediately, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it would shake me. I'm in year one, and the whole path I'm on, internships and a junior job, could be gone before I'd hit it. I'd be anxious about my parents too, because if schools and ferries get cut back as the economy shifts, their pay could be affected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get as good as I can at working with the tools, and build something people depend on, like the rota app but bigger. I'd also open a savings account with any tutoring money. And I'd go to every student meeting about it and join the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also strangely alive. It's like standing at the top of a hill on a bike. I can't see the bottom, but I'm not ready to get off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build, if you had two years to build something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the jobs go, I think what's left is the stuff that's about people: care, teaching, running places. The coding club makes me think teaching will matter. I wouldn't say that to Mum, who's a teaching assistant, because she'd worry that I'm turning into a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dad that the ferry will probably stay human for a while, since the robots come three years later. He'd laugh and say he's been replaced by a better engine for thirty years already. That's the kind of thing we say to each other.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest thing** in my lifetime and we have no plan.
I'd push for **public ownership** of the main systems and immediate income support.
think: The **junior-job path** I'm on could vanish before I reach it.
My parents' pay could be hit if schools and ferries **cut back**.
do: Get as good as I can at **working with the tools**.
Build something people **depend on**, bigger than the rota app.
Join the **student union** and go to every meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** but strangely alive, like standing at the top of a hill on a bike.
S2.quote: If the jobs go, I think what's left is the stuff that's about people: care, teaching, running places.
fieldNote: Vera's **adaptive** side shows: she turns fear into a plan to build, learn and organise.
She expects **human-centred work** to hold value, and her coding club is her evidence.
She keeps a warm, joking tone with her dad, which hides how much is at stake.

steps.text: Build a bigger scheduling app for local charities
Put every tutoring payment into a savings account
Join the students' union campaign on AI
Write to the local councillor about public ownership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a countdown, so let's use it. Five years is long enough for governments to build income support and for schools to teach this properly. I'd say it online, in the group chat, and to the kids at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be uneasy but optimistic. I'd graduate around 2029, work for two years, then everything changes. I'd feel lucky to have time. I think I'd be one of the people who can ride the wave rather than get hit by it, but I know that's not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and look for a job at a company that already uses AI in a serious way. I'd save aggressively for two years. And I'd keep teaching, because if I end up changing careers, teaching others is a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A sort of fizzy calm. I'd feel more worried for people who are further into their careers and have mortgages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your parents understand it. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably help Mum and Dad understand it. Dad's company will start bringing in diagnostic software on the ferries, and he'll hate it. I could show him how to use it as his assistant instead of his boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about your dad's timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd also think about the ferry company. In the five-year version, Dad has maybe 10 more years until retirement. Robots hit hands-on work around 2034. He'd be just short of the finish line, and that's what I'd worry about.

say: I'd say it's a **countdown**, so let's use it.
I'd tell kids at the club that **learning to teach** is a skill.
think: I'd feel **lucky to have time**, and I think I could ride the wave.
I'd worry more about people with **mortgages** than for myself.
do: Finish the degree and join a company **already using AI** seriously.
**Save aggressively** for the two working years.
Keep **teaching**, as a bridge if I change careers.
S3.quote: I think I'd be one of the people who can ride the wave rather than get hit by it, but I know that's not guaranteed.
fieldNote: Vera is **optimistic with open eyes**: she says it's not guaranteed.
She plans to be a **bridge** for her parents, helping Dad use diagnostic software.
The thought about her dad's retirement shows the real stake is her family's timing.

steps.text: Save aggressively for the two working years
Apply to companies that already use AI seriously
Teach Dad to use the ferry's diagnostic software
Keep teaching coding to children as a second skill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for a really good plan, and honestly I'd hope my generation gets to design it. I'd say we should use the time to try new things, like shorter weeks, and see what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel excited and a little nervous. I'd be 28 and maybe running something of my own by then. Ten years is long enough to take risks and fail once. I'd rather try early, while mistakes are cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work in a small company for a few years, and start a side project with real users. Maybe a service for charities, like the food bank one. I'd put a bit of money away each month, and take one or two cheap risks along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. A long runway makes me feel like I could try anything. I'd still feel sorry for anyone who's near retirement and doesn't know what happens to their pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of risk would you take with ten years ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk I'd take is probably quitting a job to try a startup. I'd only do it with six months of savings, because Mum and Dad can't bail me out. It's a pretty clear line for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the kids at your coding club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my coding club kids that nobody knows what jobs will exist, so learn how to learn. They'd say 'okay' and ask if we can play a game, which is the correct response.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** for a good plan, and my generation should help design it.
I'd say we should **try new things**, like shorter weeks.
think: I'd be **excited** and a little nervous, and ten years lets me fail once.
I'd rather try **early**, while mistakes are cheap.
do: Finish the degree and work in a **small company**.
Start a **side project** with real users, maybe for charities.
Save a little **each month** as a six-month cushion.
feel: **Calm** and curious, with a long runway.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to take risks and fail once. I'd rather try early, while mistakes are cheap.
fieldNote: Vera sees the longer timeline as **permission to experiment**.
She sets a clear line for risk: **six months of savings**, since her parents can't bail her out.
Her advice to the kids, learn how to learn, mirrors her own approach.

steps.text: Start a side service for charities with real users
Build six months of living costs in savings
Put a little money each month into a student account
Keep trying new AI tools as soon as they appear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because two years doesn't leave room for a plan or for my parents to adjust. It's not that I'm scared of the tools, it's that society wouldn't be ready. What would help is public support set up before it's needed, and schools that teach people to work with the tools instead of banning them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people my age are sometimes called lazy or entitled, and I think we're mostly trying to work out what's worth learning. I'd like somebody to ask us that more often, honestly.

headlineQuote: People my age are sometimes called lazy or entitled, and I think we're mostly trying to work out what's worth learning.
portrait: Vera is an **18-year-old** software engineering student who runs a coding club and uses AI tools every day.
Her parents, a ferry mechanic and a teaching assistant, pay **part of her costs** while she shares a flat.
She is progressive and adaptive, favouring **shorter weeks**, worker say and public ownership.
She stays calm or only uneasy across scenarios, because she builds a **plan** and checks the tools' work.
Her real worries are for **others**: her gran, her dad's timeline and people who can't learn the tools.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, because society and her parents wouldn't have time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Public support** set up early, and schools that teach people to work with the tools.
